# Task: Entity Builder & Blender Asset Pipeline

> **Target client:** native Python `client/` (wgpu-py + GLFW + imgui-bundle), per `.github/prompts/wgpu-py-migration.prompt.md`. This task builds on `level-editor.prompt.md`'s launcher (`client/engine/launcher.py`), asset preview (`client/engine/asset_preview.py`), and template-editing panel (`area_viewer.py`'s `_draw_template_section`) — read those before writing any code. It also builds directly on the just-added `tools/convert_mesh.py` (Step 9 socket extraction) and `tools/convert_animation.py`, calling both as in-process Python functions, never as subprocesses.

Right now, building a multi-part entity (e.g. a bird with body/legs/wings/beak) means: hand-run `convert_mesh.py` once per part, hand-run `convert_animation.py` once per animated part, hand-write the entity-definition JSON's `parts` array (id/mesh/material_id/`attachTo`/`localOffset`/`animation_id`/`action_animations`) by copying the shape of an example fixture, and hand-author material JSON referencing hand-packed param maps. Every step works, but none of it is discoverable or connected — this task gives it one home: a window, reachable from the launcher, that runs the conversion scripts, assembles the parts list with real validation against real socket data, assigns materials, and previews the live result, all without leaving the tool or hand-editing JSON.

**This is a builder for entity-definition JSON and material JSON. It is not a general asset importer, not a texture painter, and not a Blender replacement.** Blender authoring (modeling, pivot placement, socket empties, keyframing — see the "how to animate" walkthrough already given informally, which this task's docs step formalizes) stays exactly as documented; this tool starts at "I have exported `.glb` files," not before.

| In scope | Out of scope |
| --- | --- |
| New `client/engine/entity_builder.py`, reachable from the launcher | Extending `asset_preview.py` in place (it's deliberately read-only — see its own docstring) or bolting a fourth mode onto `area_viewer.py` (already large, mixes in Area/zone concerns this tool has no use for) |
| Orbit-camera preview of the assembled entity (shared code with `asset_preview.py`, not duplicated) | Area placement, zones, the transform gizmo, undo/redo across a full session — `area_viewer.py`'s job, unchanged |
| Import Mesh / Import Animation panels calling `convert_mesh.convert()` / `convert_animation.convert()` in-process, with a "Search..." button (`tkinter.filedialog`, stdlib) to browse to a file anywhere on disk and copy it into `pending/` — see the reversed decision noted under Constraints | A file *save* dialog, or browsing to anything other than a mesh/animation source file — this tool's other outputs (mesh/material/entity JSON) always write to fixed, predictable paths, never a user-chosen location |
| Part CRUD: add/remove a part, assign its mesh, assign `attachTo`/socket (validated against the parent part's *real* sockets, not free text), `localOffset` | Skeletal/skinned meshes — this engine has no skinning system at all, and none is added here |
| Reused per-part field editing (`dangle`, `animation_id`, `action_animations`) — refactored out of `area_viewer.py`, not copy-pasted | Multi-node-per-animation import, non-LINEAR interpolation support — `convert_animation.py`'s existing narrow scope is unchanged by this task |
| "Scaffold Parts from Sockets" — suggests part/socket pairings by naming convention, always user-confirmed before anything is written | Auto-writing parts with no confirmation step, ever — every write in this tool is explicit, matching `area_viewer.py`'s own template-edit precedent |
| Material assignment: pick an albedo + up to 4 param-map channel images, pack via `pack_param_map.pack()`, write `material-<id>.json` | **Live in-editor texture/param-map painting** — real scope, deliberately deferred; see Step 11 for the forward-looking design notes this task must leave behind for it |
| Animation clip assignment + playback preview (scrub/play/loop), reusing `sample_transform_clip`/`AnimationController` | A new clip player/animation curve editor — reuse what exists, do not build a second one |

If a request during implementation falls in the right column, it's a follow-up task, not scope creep to absorb here.

## Constraints

- No new pip dependencies. `PIL`/`wgpu`/`imgui-bundle`/`tkinter` (stdlib) already cover every need here (image loading for texture pickers, GPU preview, UI, the native file-open dialog below).
- **Reversed decision, by direct request: `tkinter.filedialog` is used for a "Search..." file-open button on both Import panels.** The original reasoning against it (`distribution.prompt.md` excludes `tkinter` from the packaged game build) doesn't actually hold: that prompt file is written entirely against the old, now-deleted PyWebView/JS client (`main.py`'s PyWebView entry point, `frontend/js/`) and is itself still "Not started" per `ROADMAP.md` — and regardless, `entity_builder.py` is a dev-only authoring tool, never part of any shipped game executable, so nothing about its imports affects a packaged build's size. The `pending/` directory-scan-and-list pattern (Step 2) is unchanged and still the *primary* way files get discovered — "Search..." is an additional, native way to get a file *into* `pending/` in the first place (it copies the picked file there via `_copy_into_pending()`, then the rest of the Import flow proceeds exactly as if the file had been dropped in manually), not a parallel mechanism that bypasses `pending/` entirely.
- `client/engine/entity_builder.py` is engine-layer, same reasoning as `level-editor.prompt.md`'s reclassification banner for `area_viewer.py`/`launcher.py`: nothing in this tool is game-specific.
- `convert_mesh.convert()`/`convert_animation.convert()`/`pack_param_map.pack()` are called as in-process Python function calls, never `subprocess`/shell-out — they're already plain functions with exactly this signature.
- Do not modify `convert_mesh.py`'s or `convert_animation.py`'s narrow refusal behavior (single mesh/primitive, single animated node, LINEAR-only interpolation) to "helpfully" work around it from the GUI. If a dropped export fails, show the exact `ConvertError` message — the CLI and the GUI must fail identically on the same bad input.
- Template writes (entity-definition JSON, material JSON) follow `area_viewer.py`'s existing pattern exactly: buffered local edits, one explicit "Confirm & Save" action per unit of work, immediate in-process `build_manifest.build_manifest()` refresh afterward. Do not invent a second persistence mechanism or an autosave.
- Follow PEP 8 (79 cols, 4-space indent) per `CLAUDE.md`.

Extract it into a new small module, `client/engine/orbit_camera.py`, with zero behavior change. Update `asset_preview.py` to import it from there. This task's own preview (Step 3) imports the same class — do not copy its ~40 lines a second time.
2. **The per-part field-editing UI** currently lives inline in `area_viewer.py`'s `_draw_template_section()` (dangle fields, `localOffset.position` fields, `action_animations` per-registered-action fields, the "Confirm & Save Template" button and its write-back). Extract the per-part body (everything from the `dangle`/`localOffset`/`action_animations` widgets through the save button, operating on one `part` dict plus a `buffer` dict) into a shared function — e.g. `draw_part_fields(part: dict, buffer: dict, action_registry, buffer_key: str) -> dict | None` returning the edited part dict when "Confirm & Save" is pressed, `None` otherwise — in a new small module (`client/engine/entity_template_editing.py`, or alongside `editor_commands.py` if that reads more naturally once you see the actual code). Do not touch `convert_mesh.py`/`convert_animation.py` in this step — they're already correct and already tested against real fixtures.

Verify: `area_viewer.py`'s existing template-editing behavior (open an entity with `parts`, edit a part's dangle value, confirm, reopen a different entity sharing the same template, see the change) is byte-identical to before the extraction — this step is a pure refactor, not a behavior change.

## Step 3 — New File: `client/engine/entity_builder.py` (Window Bootstrap) ✅

Modeled directly on `asset_preview.py`'s `run()` shape (renderer init, `ImguiRenderer`, an orbit camera, a blocking `renderer.run(draw)` loop, a "Back to Launcher" deferred-close pattern — reuse that exact fix, don't reproduce the frame-bracket crash `level-editor.prompt.md` Step 3/7 already found and fixed once), but building up a **new** entity definition (or editing an existing one, passed in like `asset_preview.run(asset_id, asset_type)`) instead of read-only viewing.

1. `run(entity_id: str | None) -> bool` — `entity_id=None` starts a blank definition (`{"parts": []}`, not yet saved anywhere); an existing id loads it via `load_entity_definition()` (same helper `area_viewer.py`'s `_draw_template_section` already uses) for editing. Returns the same "back to launcher" bool convention as `asset_preview.run()`.
2. Live preview: a `Scene` with one entity whose `render_template` points at a throwaway synthetic definition file mirroring the in-progress `parts` list (same trick `asset_preview.py`'s `_write_synthetic_definition()` already uses for raw mesh/material previews — reuse or closely mirror it) rewritten and reloaded every time the part list changes, so adding/removing a part or changing an `attachTo` is visible immediately.
3. `orbit_camera.OrbitCamera` (Step 1) for viewing the assembled entity from any angle.
4. Panel layout: a "Parts" list panel (Step 5), an "Import" panel (Step 4), a "Materials" panel (Step 7), and reuses the extracted `draw_part_fields()` (Step 1) per selected part for `dangle`/`localOffset`/`action_animations`/animation playback (Step 8).
5. A short in-window help panel or tooltip pointing at where to drop Blender exports (`frontend/assets/pending/models|animations/`, per Step 2) — this tool has no value if a first-time user doesn't know where to put files.
6. **Real additions, per direct request, not in this step's original scope**: the window launches maximized (`glfw.maximize_window(renderer.canvas._window)`, called from this tool's own `run()` -- not `renderer.init_renderer()` itself, which every other tool also calls and none of which asked to launch maximized); top/bottom menu bars (`_draw_menu_bar`/`_draw_bottom_bar`, F11 to toggle the top one) mirroring `area_viewer.py`'s own of the same name -- File (Save/Save As fold, Import Mesh/Import Animation submenus, Back to Launcher, Exit), a **Parts** menu (Scaffold Parts from Sockets submenu), and View (per-panel visibility toggles), plus an always-visible bottom strip (Mode/part count/`camera.position`); and a right-docked, tabbed **sidebar** (`_draw_sidebar`, generic -- a uniform `(scene, state, action_registry)` tab-content signature so future panels fold in by appending one `_SIDEBAR_TABS` entry) sized to match the Playback window's own current width (captured each frame Playback renders), holding Parts and Materials as its two tabs.
7. **Fixed two real reported bugs, found via an actual "nothing renders" report, not theorized:**
   - `entity_renderer.py`'s `_draw_mesh_part` used to skip the draw call entirely whenever no material handle was available (`if not handle: return False`) -- meaning any part with no `material_id` (every part `"+ Add Part"`/`"Scaffold Parts from Sockets"` create, since materials aren't derivable from geometry) rendered as nothing, no error, indistinguishable from the mesh itself having failed to load. Fixed with `MaterialLoader.get_fallback_handle()` -- a lazily-built, shared solid-magenta placeholder (the conventional "missing texture" signal), used whenever `material_id` is unset or its file fails to load. A correctly-assigned material is unaffected. This is engine-layer (`material_loader.py`/`entity_renderer.py`), not builder-only, so it also fixes the same silent-invisibility gap for `area_viewer.py`/`asset_preview.py`/any hand-authored entity missing a `material_id`.
   - Even with meshes correctly drawing, a realistically-scaled "1 unit = 1 meter" model (e.g. a ~0.13-unit-radius bird part) was still practically invisible: `OrbitCamera`'s fixed ~200-unit default radius is inherited from this engine's old pixel-tile-scale content (`MOVE_SPEED=200`, a 64-unit crate mesh) and was never migrated. Fixed with `mesh_bounding_radius()`/`entity_bounding_radius()` (pure, headlessly-tested helpers reading vertex extents straight off mesh JSON, no GPU needed) -- `_sync_preview_definition()` now auto-fits `orbit.radius` and `scene.camera`'s `near`/`far` to whatever's actually loaded on every parts-list edit, rather than assuming a fixed scale. Verified against real fixtures at two very different native scales: `entity-example-staff` (old-scale, radius ~120) auto-fits to `orbit.radius=360.4`/`near=1.2`/`far=6006.7`, exactly matching the `radius*3`/`radius*0.01`/`radius*50` formula; a real converted bird part measured radius ~0.13.
   - **Third bug, found immediately after the previous fix shipped, in the same shared camera class**: `client/engine/orbit_camera.py`'s `OrbitCamera._on_wheel` had its own fixed `20.0`-`2000.0` clamp and fixed `+/-0.5`-per-scroll-unit additive step, also sized for old-scale content. Once the auto-fit above could start the camera at a radius well under 1.0, the very first scroll (either direction) snapped the radius up to the 20.0 floor -- and the user could never scroll back in past it, reported directly as "scrolling out locks you out of scrolling back in." Fixed in the shared class itself (not per-caller): widened to a scale-agnostic `0.01`-`100000.0` clamp, and switched from an additive step to a multiplicative one (`radius *= 1.15 ** (dy/100)`, calibrated against `rendercanvas`'s GLFW backend reporting `dy ~= +/-100` per scroll notch) so the felt zoom speed stays proportional to the current distance at any scale instead of a fixed absolute step that's imperceptible at radius 2000 and a huge relative jump at radius 0.5. Being in the shared class, this also fixes the same lockout for `asset_preview.py`.
8. **New feature, per direct request: View > Mesh > Solid/Wireframe.** WebGPU has no native polygon/wireframe fill mode (unlike OpenGL/Vulkan/D3D's `PolygonMode::Line`) -- real new engine-layer rendering capability, not a settings flag: `Mesh.load()` (`client/engine/mesh.py`) now also builds `wireframe_index_buffer`/`wireframe_index_count`, a companion line-list index buffer (2 indices per triangle edge, shared edges duplicated rather than deduplicated -- simpler than an edge-adjacency structure, harmless overdraw for a debug view) built from the existing triangle indices at load time. `shader_cache.create_mesh_wireframe_pipeline()`/`ShaderCache.get_mesh_wireframe_pipeline()` compile a second pipeline reusing the solid mesh pipeline's exact `vs_main` (MVP transform, unmodified) paired with a trivial flat-white fragment shader and `line-list` topology. `EntityRenderer.set_wireframe(enabled)` is a plain instance flag; `_draw_mesh_part` swaps pipeline *and* index buffer/count together (they must always change as a pair) when it's set. The View menu's new "Mesh" submenu holds "Solid"/"Wireframe" as two mutually-exclusive items (each sets an explicit value on click, not a toggle, so the active one always shows a checkmark) -- `run()`'s `draw()` reapplies `state.wireframe` to the live preview renderer every frame (not just on click), since `_sync_preview_definition()` destroys/recreates that renderer on every parts-list edit and would otherwise silently reset it to solid.

Verify: opening the tool with `entity_id=None` shows an empty parts list and an empty preview; opening it with an existing multi-part entity id (e.g. a saved bird definition) shows all its parts assembled and rendered correctly, matching how `asset_preview.py` already renders that same entity today. Confirmed live: the window reports `MAXIMIZED` true and fills the monitor's work area; the sidebar's width tracks a real, non-default captured Playback width (387px in one live run, not the 400px fallback); a part with no `material_id` now issues a real draw call (confirmed via a direct `_draw_mesh_part` call returning `True` instead of `False`) using the magenta fallback; `orbit.radius`/`scene.camera` near/far confirmed live against real GPU state to match the auto-fit formula exactly; `OrbitCamera` confirmed numerically to zoom from `radius=0.5` down past `0.023` and back out past `1.5` across repeated scroll-in/scroll-out sequences with no floor lockout, and legacy-scale zoom (`radius=200`) confirmed to still feel comparable to the old step size; the wireframe pipeline confirmed to compile and validate against a real GPU device, a real crate mesh's 36 triangle indices confirmed to produce exactly 72 wireframe indices, `_draw_mesh_part` confirmed issuing real draw calls in both modes and switching cleanly between them, and a live run toggling `state.wireframe` mid-session confirmed the change reaches the running preview renderer and renders correctly for 10+ frames before switching back.

## Step 4 — Import Mesh / Import Animation Panels ✅

Wraps `convert_mesh.py`/`convert_animation.py` directly — the "house all the scripts for mesh or any Blender export conversions" requirement.

1. **Import Mesh panel**: lists files from `frontend/assets/pending/models/` (Step 2). Selecting one and clicking "Convert" prompts for an output mesh id (text field, pre-filled from the filename stem) and calls `convert_mesh.convert(input_path, f"frontend/assets/data/mesh/mesh-{id}.json")` in-process. On `ConvertError`, show the exact message in the panel (a status/error text area) — do not catch-and-reinterpret it. On success, refresh the manifest (`build_manifest.build_manifest()`) so the new mesh is immediately available to Step 5's mesh picker.
2. **Import Animation panel**: same shape, for `frontend/assets/pending/animations/`, calling `convert_animation.convert(input_path, f"frontend/assets/data/animation/animation-transform-{id}.json", clip_id=..., animation_name=..., loop=...)`. Expose `--animation`/`--id`/`--no-loop`'s equivalents as simple fields (a text field for the animation name, shown only if the file's animations can be listed — `convert_animation._select_animation`'s ambiguity error already lists them, so a first "probe" call can populate a dropdown instead of a blind retry loop; a checkbox for loop).
3. Converted meshes/animations become immediately selectable in Step 5's mesh picker and Step 8's animation-clip picker respectively — no separate "refresh" step beyond the manifest rebuild already done in tasks 1/2.
4. **Real addition, built alongside this step, not originally scoped in this file**: multi-mesh glTF exports (a whole rigid-part rig exported as one file — the actual, real-world common case, not the exception) can't go through `convert_mesh.convert()` directly, since it refuses anything but a single mesh, by design (see that module's own docstring). A separate agent built `tools/split_glb.py` for exactly this — one multi-mesh `.glb` in, one single-mesh `.glb` per mesh-bearing node out (materials/textures dropped, since this project's mesh pipeline never reads glTF materials anyway), defaulting its output into `frontend/assets/pending/models/<source stem>/`, a subfolder of Step 2's own pending directory. The Import Mesh panel gained a second button, "Split Multi-Mesh GLB," next to "Convert Mesh," calling `split_glb.split_glb(input_path, output_dir=None, mesh_dir=str(MESH_DIR), do_convert=...)`. This required widening the mesh-file listing helper (`_pending_model_files()`) to scan one level of subdirectories under `pending/models/`, not just its top level, so split output shows up in the same picker. **`do_convert` reversed from `False` to `True`, per direct request ("when splitting meshes, also automatically convert them")** — originally `False` deliberately, so each part still needed an individual "Convert Mesh" click with a user-chosen id; now each split part converts immediately, with its id derived from `split_glb.py`'s own sanitized Blender-object-name convention rather than a per-part prompt. Since `split_glb.split_glb()` catches and prints its own per-part `ConvertError` internally rather than raising or returning a success flag (so one bad part doesn't abort the whole split), the wrapper checks each expected output mesh JSON's existence on disk to know which parts actually converted.
5. **Real addition, per direct request: a "Search..." button on both Import panels**, opening the native OS file-open dialog (`_browse_for_file()`, `tkinter.filedialog` — see the reversed "no tkinter" decision under Constraints) filtered to `.glb`/`.gltf`. Picking a file copies it into the relevant pending directory (`_copy_into_pending()`, renaming on a name collision rather than overwriting an unrelated file, a no-op if the picked file already lives there) and pre-fills the file combo/output-id field with it — the rest of the Convert/Split flow is completely unaware whether a file arrived by manual drop or by this button. Every message this button produces (and every other action in this tool) also fires a bottom-left toast (`_show_toast()`/`_draw_toast()`, 3-second auto-expiry) — a later, separately-requested addition to this same file, not scoped in the original Step 4 text either.
6. **Real relocation, per direct request: no standalone "Import" window anymore.** `_draw_import_panel` was split into two content-only functions (`_draw_import_mesh_content`/`_draw_import_animation_content`, no `imgui.begin()`/`end()` of their own) and folded into the File menu as "Import Mesh"/"Import Animation" submenus (Step 10) — the same "submenu holding real widgets" pattern `File > Save As` already established, not a plain `menu_item` (both need file combos/text fields/buttons, not a single click action). The View menu's "Import" visibility toggle was removed along with the window it toggled.
7. **Real addition, per direct request: "when a mesh is converted, add it to the entity."** Both Convert Mesh and (now-auto-converting) Split Multi-Mesh GLB call `_add_part_for_converted_mesh(scene, state, mesh_id)` on success — a new, unattached part (`{"id": ..., "mesh": mesh_id}`) is appended to `state.parts` for the freshly-converted mesh, with `_sync_preview_definition()` run immediately so it's visible right away. The part's id defaults to the mesh id with its `mesh-` prefix stripped (`mesh_id_to_part_id()`), deduplicated the same way Scaffold's ids always were (`unique_part_id()`, extracted to a shared function for this). **Deliberately a no-op, not a duplicate part, when a part already references that exact mesh id** — a re-conversion (e.g. re-exporting after a Blender fix) shouldn't pile up a second part every time; `_draw_import_mesh_content`'s toast reflects whichever happened (mentions the added part id, or just the reconversion message, with no mention of a part).
8. This interacts with Step 6's Scaffold panel: since Import/Split now routinely leave unattached parts sitting in `state.parts` already, Scaffold was updated (Step 6 task 6) to *attach* an existing matching unattached part rather than creating a duplicate — read that task, not just this one, to understand the full mesh-import-to-wired-entity flow.

Verify: importing a valid single-part mesh export produces the exact same JSON `convert_mesh.py` would produce from the CLI (byte-for-byte, given the same input); importing an export with two animated nodes shows `convert_animation.py`'s real "animation targets 2 different objects" error text, unmodified, in the panel. ## Step 5 — Part CRUD ✅

The genuinely new UI — nothing in the codebase today lets you add/remove a part or wire `attachTo` without hand-editing JSON.

1. "+ Add Part" — appends a new part `{"id": "<auto or user-typed>", "mesh": None}` to the in-progress `parts` list. The first part added has no `attachTo` option (nothing to attach to yet) and becomes the de-facto root; every part after the first must pick an `attachTo` (see task 3) — enforced by disabling parts-after-the-first from having no parent, matching `entity_renderer.py`'s own "root has no `attachTo`" convention.
2. Per part: a mesh picker (combo box over the `"meshes"` manifest category, same data source `area_viewer.py`'s asset browser already reads) and a material picker (combo box over `"materials"`, plus a "New Material..." shortcut into Step 7).
3. `attachTo` picker: a combo box of **already-added, earlier parts only** (enforces `entity_renderer.py`'s validated ordering rule directly in the UI, rather than letting the user create an invalid reference and discovering it at render time), and — once a parent part is chosen — a second combo box of **that parent mesh's real sockets** (`Mesh.get_socket`/`_sockets`, loaded the moment the parent's mesh is picked). No free-text socket names anywhere in this tool.
4. "Remove Part" — removes a part and clears any other part's `attachTo` that pointed at it (surface a warning listing which parts got orphaned; do not silently leave a dangling reference).
5. Reordering isn't a first-class drag-and-drop feature — since `attachTo` ordering matters, simplest correct behavior is: parts list stays in add-order, and a part cannot select an `attachTo` target that hasn't been added yet (task 3 already enforces this at picker-population time, so no separate reorder UI is needed for correctness).
6. **Real relocation, per direct request: no standalone "Parts" window anymore.** `_draw_part_list_panel` was split into a content-only function (`_draw_parts_tab`, no `imgui.begin()`/`end()` of its own) and folded into the right-side sidebar (Step 3's addition) as its first tab, next to Materials — the sidebar's tab-content signature was widened to a uniform `(scene, state, action_registry)` for every tab so Parts (which needs all three) and Materials (which ignores two of them) share one calling convention. The View menu's "Parts" visibility toggle was removed along with the window it toggled — visibility is the whole sidebar's toggle now ("Sidebar (Parts/Materials)").
7. **New tab, per direct request: sidebar "Meshes" — lists meshes imported into an entity.** `_draw_meshes_tab` (content-only, same pattern) lists the distinct mesh ids referenced by any of the entity's current parts (`meshes_used_by_parts()`), each with which part(s) use it (`parts_using_mesh()`) and its socket names (reusing `read_mesh_sockets()`, no new lookup). Deliberately read-only and deliberately *not* a global project-wide mesh browser (that's the Parts tab's own mesh combo, or the launcher's View Asset tab) — this answers "what geometry does *this* entity actually use," derived live from `state.parts` rather than tracked as separate import history, so it can never drift out of sync with the parts list.
8. **New tab, per direct request: sidebar "Animations" — same shape as the Meshes tab, one content type over.** `_draw_animations_tab` lists the distinct animation clip ids referenced by any part (`animations_used_by_parts()` — combines `animation_id`, the continuous/looping field, and every value in `action_animations`, the one-shot/triggered map, since both reference the same kind of transform-clip id), each annotated with which part(s) use it and *how* (`parts_using_animation()` — `"animation_id"` vs. `"action:<name>"`; a single part can reference the same clip both ways, or two different clips, and both show up correctly). Also read-only, also derived live from `state.parts` — assign/change animations from the Parts tab, preview playback from the Playback panel; this tab is purely "what's in use."

Verify: building a 3-part chain (root → child attached to root's socket → grandchild attached to child's socket) live in the tool renders identically to hand-writing the equivalent JSON (cross-check against `entity-example-staff.json`'s shape); attempting to attach a part to itself or to a not-yet-added part is impossible through the UI (not just rejected with an error). The Meshes tab confirmed live against `entity-example-staff`'s real 2 parts/2 meshes, rendering correctly for 15 frames with no crash. The Animations tab confirmed live against the same fixture's real "charm" part (which has both a continuous `animation_id` and a one-shot `action_animations` entry), rendering both usages correctly for 15 frames with no crash.

## Step 6 — "Scaffold Parts from Sockets" ✅

The automation requested for the common case: a root mesh already has all its sockets authored (per the Blender workflow), and every attaching part is a 1:1 match by naming convention.

1. Button, enabled once a root part with a mesh (and that mesh's loaded `sockets`) exists. For each socket the root mesh defines, search the `"meshes"` manifest category for a best-guess match (e.g. socket `beak_socket` → strip `_socket`, look for a mesh id containing `beak`) and show one row per socket: socket name, a combo box pre-selected to the best guess (or empty if nothing matched reasonably), and a checkbox to include/skip it.
2. "Add Selected Parts" appends one part per checked row, with `attachTo` already wired to the root + that socket, `id` defaulting to the socket name minus `_socket`, `mesh` set to whichever the combo box currently shows (the user's override, if they changed it) — then drops into the normal Step 5 part list for further editing (material, animation, etc.), never auto-saved.
3. Never guesses `material_id` or `animation_id` — those stay unset, exactly like the plain "+ Add Part" flow, per this task's original scoping (materials/animations aren't derivable from geometry).
4. **Fixed a real reported bug**: "Add Selected Parts" only ever guarded against *id* collisions (renaming `wing_l` → `wing_l_2`), never against a socket that already had a part attached — so re-running it, or scaffolding a socket someone had already attached a part to by hand, silently created a second, overlapping part at the same socket. Fixed with `part_attached_to_socket()` (a pure, headlessly-tested helper): a socket already covered shows disabled text naming the existing part instead of a checkbox/combo, and "Add Selected Parts" re-checks defensively rather than trusting the UI alone (`scaffold_state` can carry a stale `"include": True` from before a part existed at that socket).
5. **Real relocation, per direct request: no standalone "Scaffold Parts from Sockets" window anymore.** Split into a content-only function (`_draw_scaffold_content`, no `imgui.begin()`/`end()` of its own) and folded into a new top-level **"Parts"** menu-bar entry (Step 10) as a submenu — the same "submenu holding real widgets" pattern File's Save As/Import Mesh/Import Animation already established. This new Parts *menu* is for Parts-related actions (currently just Scaffold); the Parts *list* itself lives in the sidebar (task 6 of Step 5), not here.
6. **Real reconciliation needed once Step 4 started auto-adding parts on conversion (see Step 4 task 6 below)**: once Import Mesh/Split Multi-Mesh GLB routinely pre-populate the parts list with unattached parts (one per converted mesh), "Add Selected Parts" naively creating a *new* part per socket would double every part -- one unattached copy from import, one newly-created and attached copy from scaffolding, both referencing the same mesh. Fixed with `find_unattached_part_for_mesh()`: before creating a new part for a socket, look for an existing, non-root, unattached part already using the suggested mesh, and *attach that one* (mutate its `attachTo` in place, keep its existing id) instead of creating a duplicate. Each socket row now also shows which behavior a click will produce ("-> will attach existing part 'x'" vs. "-> will create a new part"), so this isn't a silent behavior change per this task's own transparency precedent. `unique_part_id()` (the id-collision dedup logic, previously inline here) was extracted to a shared pure function so this and the new mesh-conversion auto-add path (Step 4) use the identical rule.

Verify: given a root mesh with 5 sockets (`leg_l_socket`, `leg_r_socket`, `wing_l_socket`, `wing_r_socket`, `beak_socket`) and matching mesh assets already imported, the scaffold panel pre-selects all 5 correctly and "Add Selected Parts" produces exactly the 5-part list Step 5 could otherwise only build by hand, in one click plus a confirm. Confirmed end-to-end against the real 6-part bird rig: splitting the original combined `bird.glb` with auto-convert produced 6 unattached parts (one per mesh), and simulating Scaffold against them attached all 5 non-root parts to their correct sockets by *reusing* the existing parts -- final count stayed at exactly 6, not 12.

## Step 9 — Save/Persist ✅

1. "Save Entity" — writes the in-progress `parts` list to `frontend/assets/data/entity/entity-<id>.json` (prompting for an id if this is a new, unsaved definition — same pattern as `level-editor.prompt.md` Step 11's Area "Save As" prompt), via the same small persistence helper that step already built (`area_io.py` or wherever it landed) — do not write a second, parallel entity-JSON-writing function.
2. Immediately calls `build_manifest.build_manifest()` and rewrites `manifest.json`, exactly like every other save path in this codebase (`level-editor.prompt.md` Step 11 point 3) — a newly-built entity must be immediately visible in the launcher's "View Asset → Entities" tab and in `area_viewer.py`'s asset browser with no manual rebuild step.
3. Material JSON (Step 7) is already saved incrementally as each material is packed — "Save Entity" only needs to persist the entity-definition JSON itself, which merely *references* material ids already on disk.
4. **Real bug found and fixed, reported directly as "saving names it `entity-entity-<name>`" and "saving did not save the parts"** — both symptoms of one root cause in `area_io.py` itself, not something this file introduced: every *other* "entity asset id" in this codebase (manifest keys, `asset_loader.register()` keys, `entity.render_template` field values) is the **prefixed** form (`"entity-<name>"` — every real entity-definition file lacks an explicit `"id"` field, so `tools/build_manifest.py`'s `json_asset_id()` falls back to the full filename stem, prefix included), but `save_entity_definition()`/`load_entity_definition()` alone expected the **bare** form and unconditionally prepended `entity-`. Reopening a saved entity via the launcher's "Edit" button (which passes the manifest-derived, prefixed id) fed a prefixed id back into these functions: `load_entity_definition("entity-bird")` looked for a nonexistent `entity-entity-bird.json`, silently returned `None`, and `state.parts` started **empty** even though the real file had real parts — and the next "Save" then wrote to that same wrong double-prefixed path, orphaning the original file entirely. Fixed with `area_io.normalize_entity_id()` (strips a leading `entity-` if present, so the convention is idempotent regardless of which form a caller holds) applied inside both functions, plus `save_entity_definition()` now stamping the written JSON's own `"id"` field with the correct, resolved value so future manifest scans never need the stem-fallback at all. `entity_builder.py`'s `run()` also normalizes `entity_id` immediately on entry, so `state.entity_id` is always displayed consistently regardless of whether the entity was opened via "Save As" or the launcher's "Edit". **Being a fix to the shared `area_io.py`, not `entity_builder.py`-only, this also retroactively fixes the identical dormant bug in `area_viewer.py`'s own "Confirm & Save Template" flow** (which passes `entity.render_template` — always the prefixed form — straight into these same functions) — a bug `level-editor.prompt.md`'s own Phase 14 status notes already flagged as unverified by real clicks, and which turns out to have been real.

Verify: saving a newly-built entity, then opening it from the launcher's "View Asset" (read-only `asset_preview.py`) immediately afterward, with no manual manifest rebuild, shows the identical assembled result this tool's own preview showed. Confirmed live and by direct reproduction: constructing a scratch entity, saving it with a bare id, then reloading and re-saving with the *prefixed* form (simulating a real launcher round-trip) recovers the real parts on load and overwrites the original file correctly on save, with zero double-prefixed file created. A live boot passing the prefixed id directly into `run()` (exactly as `launcher.py`'s "Edit" button would) confirmed `state.entity_id` normalizes to the bare form and both real parts (`shaft`/`charm`, with their full `dangle`/`animation_id`/`action_animations` data intact) load correctly.

## Step 13 — Animation Editor: "New Animation" + Multi-Part Rig Clips ✅

Per direct request: a button on the Animations tab to name and create an empty animation, and an "edit mode" that opens a dedicated editor window with a horizontal scrollable keyframe strip, per-keyframe part assignment, and per-part position/rotation/scale editing.

This is a genuinely new *runtime* clip shape, not just new editor UI — confirmed with the user before building (see the two `AskUserQuestion` decisions this step is built against): until now, one `transform_clip.py` JSON file always drove exactly one part (a part points at a clip via its own `animation_id`). "Assign different parts to a keyframe, each with its own transform" needs one clip to drive *several* parts on one shared timeline — a new "multi-part rig clip" shape, added as a strict, backward-compatible extension of the existing schema, not a new file format. The third transform type was confirmed to mean **scale**, not real shear/skew — this engine has no shear math anywhere (`mat4.py`, the WGSL shaders) and building it was out of scope for what was actually being asked.

1. **`client/engine/transform_clip.py` (runtime schema + sampler, engine-layer, not builder-only)**: a keyframe may now hold a `"parts"` map (`{part_id: {"position"/"rotation"/"scale": [...]}}` ) instead of top-level position/rotation/scale fields. `sample_transform_clip()` gained a `part_id: Optional[str]` parameter — when given, and *any* keyframe in the clip defines a `"parts"` map, sampling filters to just that part's own keyframes (interpolating only across the keyframes that actually name it, holding at the nearest one outside that span — same "hold at the bracketing keyframe" rule the original flat schema already used) and the clip's flat top-level fields are ignored. A clip with no `"parts"` map anywhere is unaffected regardless of whether a caller passes `part_id` — the two existing hand-authored clips (`charm-spin`/`charm-activate-swing`) needed no migration and are exercised unchanged by the existing regression tests. The clip's *own* loop-wrap duration is still based on its full last keyframe (not a per-part filtered subset), so every part in a shared rig clip stays on one common clock even if individual parts' own tracks end earlier.
2. **`client/engine/entity_renderer.py`**: `_sample_part_animation()`/`_sample_part_action_animation()` (which already have `part_id` in scope) now forward it into both `sample_transform_clip()` calls — the only change needed for real gameplay entities to actually play a multi-part rig clip correctly; every other consumer of these two methods is unaffected.
3. **`client/engine/entity_builder.py`, Animations tab — "New Animation"**: a name field + "Create" button. Rejects an empty name or a name whose output file (`animation-transform-<name>.json`) already exists (no silent overwrite). On success: writes an empty clip (`new_animation_clip()` — `id`/`type`/`loop` set, `keyframes: []`, no default first keyframe so an untouched new clip has no opinion about what it should hold), refreshes the manifest, and immediately opens it in the Animation Editor (see task 4) — since a brand-new clip has no part usage yet, it won't itself appear in the tab's own "animations used by this part" list (deliberately unchanged scope, still not a global project-wide animation browser) until Save actually assigns it to a part, so auto-opening the editor is the only way to reach a just-created clip before then. Each already-listed clip also gained an "Edit" button.
4. **New window: the Animation Editor** (`_draw_animation_editor_window`, opened via `_open_animation_editor` — always reloads the clip fresh off disk, never off `EntityRenderer`'s own permanent per-clip cache, same reasoning as `_sync_preview_definition`'s cache-invalidation workaround). Layout: a `loop` checkbox and "Add Keyframe" button; below that, a horizontally-scrollable child window of one button per keyframe (labeled by its own `time_ms`, highlighted when selected) — `imgui.begin_child(..., window_flags=WindowFlags_.horizontal_scrollbar)`, satisfying "horizontal scrollable menu for keyframes" directly, not a plain vertical list. Selecting a keyframe shows: a "gap from previous (ms)" drag-float (editing relative spacing, not raw absolute `time_ms`, is the natural authoring unit — see `keyframe_gap()`/`set_keyframe_gap()`, which moves only that one keyframe's own time, leaving every later keyframe's own stored time untouched so its *gap* from the now-shifted keyframe changes instead of the whole tail silently shifting), a "Delete Keyframe" button, one collapsing header per part currently assigned to it with `drag_float3` position/rotation/scale fields and a "Remove from keyframe" button, and (if any of this entity's parts aren't yet in this keyframe) a combo + "Assign to Keyframe" button. "Save" writes the clip back to its original path, then calls `stamp_animation_id_for_assigned_parts()` — every part referenced anywhere in the clip that doesn't already have its own `animation_id` gets one stamped to this clip id, so assigning a part to a keyframe is by itself enough to make it actually play, with no separate trip to the Parts tab; a part that already has a different (or the same) `animation_id` is never overwritten, so the Animation Editor can't silently steal a part away from a clip it was deliberately assigned to elsewhere. Nothing touches disk until Save — same buffer-then-explicit-save shape as every other edit in this tool (no undo stack, per this file's own docstring).
5. Pure, headlessly-tested helpers backing all of the above (no imgui/GPU): `new_animation_clip_id`/`new_animation_clip_path`/`new_animation_clip`, `default_keyframe_transform`, `add_keyframe`/`remove_keyframe`, `keyframe_gap`/`set_keyframe_gap`, `assign_part_to_keyframe`/`remove_part_from_keyframe`, `parts_assigned_in_clip`, `stamp_animation_id_for_assigned_parts`.
6. **Live pose preview, per direct follow-up request ("make the rendered mesh update to the transformation being applied to a part in the currently selected keyframe")**: `apply_keyframe_preview(parts, keyframe)` returns a copy of the entity's parts list where every part *keyframe* assigns a transform to has its `localOffset` replaced by that keyframe's own position/rotation/scale, with `animation_id`/`action_animations` stripped from the copy -- without stripping those, a part that already has a real running animation (e.g. `charm`'s continuous spin) would have its live-sampled pose silently override the static preview pose the very next frame, exactly like it already overrides `localOffset` at real render time (`entity_renderer.py`'s `_draw_entity` reads `localOffset` as the baseline, then layers any live animation sample on top -- this reuses that exact existing mechanism rather than adding a second, parallel transform-application path). `_sync_preview_definition` now builds this overridden copy (reading `state.animation_editor_clip`/`animation_editor_selected_kf`) and writes *that* to the scratch preview file instead of `state.parts` directly -- `state.parts` itself is never touched, so the previewed pose can never leak into a real "Save Entity". Every interaction that changes the selected keyframe's identity or a previewed part's transform (selecting a different keyframe, Add/Delete Keyframe, each `drag_float3` edit, Assign/Remove-from-keyframe, and closing the editor window, which reverts the preview back to normal) calls `_sync_preview_definition` again, so the orbit-preview mesh visibly tracks the edit within the same "any edit re-syncs the live preview" convention every other panel in this file already follows.
7. **Animations table, per direct follow-up request ("include a table of animations that already exist for this entity and allow the user to select them as active")**: confirmed with the user first that "active" means "currently open in the Animation Editor" (not a separate live-preview player, and not a shortcut for assigning a part's `animation_id`) -- so this replaces the previous plain per-row text + "Edit" button with a real `imgui.begin_table`/`table_setup_column`/`table_headers_row` table (columns: Animation, Used By), where each row is a full-width `imgui.selectable` (`SelectableFlags_.span_all_columns`, so clicking anywhere in the row selects it, not just the id text). A row's selected/highlighted state is `state.editing_animation_id == animation_id` -- read fresh from state every frame, not tracked as separate row-selection state, so the table's highlight always matches whichever clip is actually open, including when opened via "New Animation" rather than a row click. Selecting a row calls the same `_open_animation_editor` the old "Edit" button called; the "Used By" column condenses `parts_using_animation()`'s per-usage roles into one compact per-row string (e.g. `"charm (loop), charm (action: activate)"`) instead of the old multi-line per-usage text block.
8. **Real bug found and fixed, reported directly as "it's not finding the flap animation I started"**: the Animations table (task 7) reads `animations_used_by_parts(state.parts)` -- it has no independent knowledge of clip files on disk, only of what the *current entity's own parts* reference. `stamp_animation_id_for_assigned_parts` (task 4's Save) only ever updated `state.parts` **in memory** -- persisting that stamp to the entity's own saved file has always required a separate, explicit File > Save. Live reproduction with the user's own real files confirmed the exact failure: `frontend/assets/data/animation/animation-transform-flap.json` existed on disk with real keyframe data correctly assigning `l_wing` a rotation, and was correctly registered in the manifest -- but `frontend/assets/data/entity/entity-bird.json` (the actual saved entity) showed `l_wing` with no `animation_id` at all, because the Animation Editor's "Save" had run (writing the clip file, confirmed by its real keyframe data) but a subsequent File > Save on the entity itself never had. The next time `bird` was loaded, `l_wing` came back with no animation_id, so the table silently lost "flap" -- it was still on disk and still in the manifest, just no longer referenced by anything. **Per direct decision** (a real design fork: this tool's established rule is that *only* File > Save ever writes `entity-<id>.json`, which a "warn more clearly, don't auto-save" fix would have preserved) -- `_save_animation_editor` now also calls `save_entity_definition({"parts": state.parts}, state.entity_id)` immediately whenever it actually stamps a part, deliberately breaking that rule for this one case since leaving the stamp unpersisted is what caused the bug; it only fires when `state.entity_id` is already set (nothing to persist to yet for a brand-new, never-saved entity -- same gate File > Save's own Save/Save As split already uses), and the toast now says explicitly whether the entity was saved or still needs a first File > Save As. The real broken file was repaired directly (`entity-bird.json`'s `l_wing` now carries `"animation_id": "anim-transform-flap"`, confirmed to make `animations_used_by_parts` return it immediately).
9. **Real bug found and fixed, reported directly as "I'm applying transformations to parts in the animation but the mesh render is not updating with the transformations"**: not a rendering bug -- reproduced live against the user's own real `bird`/`l_wing`/`anim-transform-flap` files with the same `EntityRenderer._draw_mesh_part` argument-recording technique task 6 used, and confirmed the world transform *was* being applied correctly every frame. The real cause is a scale/framing mismatch: `entity_bounding_radius` measures the whole bird at ~0.13 units, so task 6's own auto-fit formula sits the orbit camera only ~0.5 units away with a 45-degree FOV -- a visible area only ~0.2 units top-to-bottom. The user's own real `flap` clip poses `l_wing` to position `[0, 50, 2]`, ~240x past the edge of that frame -- correctly rendered every frame, just invisible, indistinguishable from "not updating." Both requested fixes implemented together, per direct decision: (a) `keyframe_preview_reach(keyframe, base_radius)` -- a new pure helper approximating how far the currently-previewed keyframe's posed parts extend from the origin (each assigned part's raw position magnitude plus `base_radius` scaled by that part's largest scale component; deliberately approximate, not an exact world-space bound through the full attachTo/socket chain, which this pure helper has no access to) -- `_sync_preview_definition`'s camera auto-fit now takes `max(entity_bounding_radius(...), keyframe_preview_reach(...))`, so a keyframe pose that moves a part far from rest widens the camera to keep it in view instead of silently exceeding the frustum; (b) `position_drag_speed(entity_radius)` -- the position `drag_float3`'s speed (units per pixel) now scales with the entity's own bounding radius (`max(entity_radius * 0.02, 0.0005)`) instead of a fixed `0.01`/px, so a short drag on a tiny model produces a small, controllable change instead of flinging a part dozens of units on a couple hundred pixels of mouse movement -- deliberately position-only: rotation (radians) and scale (a unitless multiplier) are already size-independent of the entity's physical scale, so their existing fixed speed stays correct at any scale.

Verify: 19 new headless assertions (81 total in `run_entity_builder_test.py`, all passing) cover every pure helper above plus `transform_clip.sample_transform_clip`'s new multi-part path directly (a two-part, two-keyframe synthetic rig clip: mid-interpolation for a part present in both keyframes, "hold at its only keyframe" for a part absent from the later one, `{}` for a part_id no keyframe names at all, and confirmed the flat single-part schema samples identically regardless of whether `part_id` is now passed). Live GPU verification against the real `entity-example-staff` fixture (`shaft`/`charm`) went further than a rendering-only check: it replicated "New Animation" → opened the editor → added two keyframes → assigned `shaft` to both (with different positions) and `charm` to only the first → **Save** → then re-loaded the just-written JSON off disk and ran it through the real `sample_transform_clip()` exactly as `entity_renderer.py` does, confirming correct mid-clip interpolation for `shaft` and correct "hold at last known keyframe" for `charm`. It also confirmed `stamp_animation_id_for_assigned_parts` in the same live pass: `shaft` (previously unset) was stamped with the new clip id, while `charm` (already carrying `anim-transform-charm-spin` from the fixture) was left untouched, exactly as designed. The live preview then continued rendering for 15 real frames with `shaft`'s freshly-stamped multi-part clip actually active on the real render path (not a standalone script call) with no crash, and the Animations tab's new "New Animation" controls plus the full Animation Editor window (keyframe strip, `drag_float3` fields, combo, collapsing headers) drew without error across the same 15 frames. **Task 6's live pose preview verified against the actual GPU draw call, not just the JSON it writes**: 7 new headless assertions (88 total) cover `apply_keyframe_preview` directly (overrides `localOffset` only for the assigned part, strips `animation_id`/`action_animations`, leaves an unassigned part's own dict object completely untouched, never mutates the original parts list). A second live GPU script monkeypatched `EntityRenderer._draw_mesh_part` to record the exact `world_matrix` each part is actually drawn with (the real per-frame value, not a value read back from a cache) and confirmed, in sequence against the real `shaft` part: posing it to `[3, 0, 0]` via a keyframe produced a world transform with `x == 3.0`; re-editing that same keyframe's position to `[-7, 2, 0]` (replicating a live `drag_float3` change) moved it to `x == -7.0` on a later frame with no further action needed; and closing the Animation Editor reverted it back to `x == 0.0` (its real, unset `localOffset`) -- proving both that edits reach the live mesh and that the override cleanly releases the part once editing stops. **Task 7's Animations table verified live**: no new pure helpers were needed (it reuses `animations_used_by_parts`/`parts_using_animation`/`_open_animation_editor` unchanged), so verification is a live GPU render against the real `entity-example-staff` fixture -- opened `anim-transform-charm-spin` directly (so the table renders a real selected/highlighted row, not only the unselected case), then rendered the table alongside the open Animation Editor window for 15 real frames with no crash. **Task 8's fix verified against the exact reported scenario**: a new headless integration test seeds a throwaway saved entity with one unset-animation part, opens a fresh clip in the Animation Editor, assigns that part to a keyframe, confirms the on-disk entity file has no `animation_id` yet (pre-Save), calls `_save_animation_editor`, then reloads the entity file from disk and confirms the stamped `animation_id` is now actually there -- proving the fix persists to disk, not just to `state.parts` (90 total headless assertions, all passing). A live GPU script reproduced the same sequence end-to-end through the real window plumbing (`_open_animation_editor`/`add_keyframe`/`assign_part_to_keyframe`/`_save_animation_editor`) against a throwaway entity, confirming the same before/after disk-state result outside the headless harness too. **Task 9's fix verified numerically and live against the exact reported scenario**: 7 new headless assertions (97 total, all passing) cover `keyframe_preview_reach` (0.0/no-op for no keyframe or no parts assigned, captures the real flap clip's actual ~50-unit reach rather than the bird's ~0.13-unit rest radius, and picks the largest scale component correctly) and `position_drag_speed` (well under the old fixed 0.01 for a bird-sized entity, never near-zero for a vanishingly small one, above 0.01 for old-scale legacy content). A live GPU script posed `entity-bird`'s real `l_wing` to the clip's actual far-flung `[0, 50, 2]` and confirmed `orbit.radius` widened from a baseline `0.5` (rest-pose-only fit) to over `151` and `scene.camera["far"]` widened from `100.0` to over `2500` -- the posed wing is now actually inside the visible frustum instead of ~240x past its edge.
